title: Using the Efficient “Take a Stand” Strategy to Hook Kids into a Reading
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that much of a teacher's job is motivating students to do the actual work of reading, since readers only improve by reading. He frames his position on whole-class complex texts as conditional: if teachers cannot get most students actually reading them, a choice-heavy approach makes sense, but if they can, every student deserves instruction in grappling with grade-level complex texts. Getting students to really read such texts depends heavily on how well the teacher hooks them in beforehand. He presents Take a Stand, an efficient pre-reading routine in which students physically show their degree of agreement with a debatable statement drawn from the text, explain their position briefly, and then read to find where the author takes a stand. He defends it as effective, time-efficient, and inclusive because it introduces argument, the core move of academic life, as something every student can join.
points: Stuart's badminton analogy makes motivation the central instructional problem: a reader cannot improve without actually reading, so getting students to read is much of the job.
He makes choice-heavy literacy conditional rather than ideological: it is the fallback if a teacher cannot get most students reading whole-class complex texts, not the goal.
Take a Stand turns a debatable claim or theme from the text into a statement students answer physically (stand, chair, seat, floor), then sends them into the text to find the author's own stand.
The routine is deliberately kept short, with brief three-sentence explanations, so the hook does not eat the time students need for the reading itself.
quotes: Just as a badminton player (see how inclusive I am in my analogies?) cannot get better at hitting the shuttlecock without actually hitting the shuttlecock, so also a reader cannot get better at reading without actually reading.

This is why I agree with those who advocate for a choice-heavy approach to literacy if we cannot get a firm majority of students grappling with whole-class complex texts. But the most critical word in the preceding sentence is if — if we can get all students reading the whole-class complex texts we give them, then I'd say let me earn my money teaching all of my kids, from the lowest to the highest reader, to grapple with grade-appropriate complex texts.

Whether giving kids an article of the week (Kelly Gallagher‘s idea, by the way) or Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, I'm a fool if I think even a fraction of my kids will read them — I mean really, heartfully, thoughtfully, mindfully, fully read them — apart from me hooking them in.

When previewing a text before a lesson, I try to find a debatable claim the text makes or at least a debatable theme it touches upon, and then I turn this claim or theme into a debatable statement (much like the Reading for Meaning strategy).

I then randomly call on kids or ask for volunteers to explain their stand in three sentences or less. Remember: the point of this activity is hooking kids into a text — I want to be as efficient as possible in achieving that end.
it's inclusive and fun, helping kids see that the name of the game in academia — argument — includes each of them and is naturally engaging.
